verified_facts.note: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey is the authoritative weekly tracker; rates crossed 7% in late 2022 and have remained elevated through 2023–2024

verified_facts.statement: Mortgage rates are mechanically linked to 10-year Treasury yields plus a mortgage-backed securities (MBS) spread
verified_facts.note: Standard bond-market transmission mechanism; MBS spreads typically 150–200 basis points above 10-year Treasury

verified_facts.statement: The Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate from near-zero in 2022–2023 in response to inflation
verified_facts.note: Fed funds rate raised from 0–0.25% (Dec 2021) to 5.25–5.50% (July 2023) and held through 2024

verified_facts.statement: 30-year mortgage rates in the 1980s–1990s frequently exceeded 7 percent, with peaks above 10 percent
verified_facts.note: Historical Freddie Mac data shows rates of 10%+ in 1981–1982, 8%+ in 1994–1995

verified_facts.statement: Pandemic-era mortgage rates (2020–2021) fell below 3 percent
verified_facts.note: Rates hit historic lows of 2.65–2.71% in late 2021

verified_facts.statement: Home prices in the US reached record nominal levels in 2021–2022
verified_facts.note: Case-Shiller and Zillow indices show peak nominal prices in 2022; prices have moderated but remain elevated

verified_facts.statement: Housing inventory (months of supply) declined significantly from 2020–2023
verified_facts.note: NAR data shows inventory fell from ~4 months (2020) to ~2–3 months (2023–2024)

verified_facts.statement: Existing homeowners with sub-3% mortgages have strong financial incentive not to sell and refinance at 7%
verified_facts.note: Simple arithmetic: a $300k mortgage at 2.5% costs ~$1,200/month; at 7% costs ~$2,000/month

unverified_shared_claims.statement: The US engaged in a war with Iran that directly caused oil price spikes and inflation expectations
unverified_shared_claims.note: No declared war with Iran occurred during the 2022–2024 period when rates exceeded 7%. There were escalations (e.g., Soleimani killing Jan 2020, Oct 2024 missile strikes) but no formal war declaration. Framings conflate geopolitical tension with direct causation.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Mortgage rates are 'unaffordable' for first-time buyers and millennials
unverified_shared_claims.note: Affordability is a relative and subjective measure. Verified: monthly payments are higher at 7% than at 3%; unverified: whether this constitutes structural unattainability vs. reduced but still viable homeownership for some cohorts

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Zoning and NIMBYism are the primary drivers of housing unaffordability
unverified_shared_claims.note: Widely cited in housing research but causality is debated; supply constraints are real, but their relative weight vs. demand, rates, and prices is contested

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Fed Chair Warsh has taken a 'hawkish stance' resisting Trump's rate-cut demands
unverified_shared_claims.note: Trump has publicly called for rate cuts; Warsh's actual policy positions and statements would need direct attribution to verify

points_of_disagreement: Whether 7% rates represent a crisis or a return to historical normality
Whether the primary driver is Fed policy, geopolitical shocks (Iran), structural housing supply, or the lock-in effect of existing low-rate mortgages
Whether the Iran conflict materially caused the rate rise or is a post-hoc correlation
Whether the White House or the Fed bears primary responsibility for high rates
Whether high rates are the disease or a symptom of deeper structural problems (supply, zoning)
Whether homeownership is structurally unattainable for a generation or merely more expensive than the pandemic anomaly
Whether central bank independence should yield to political pressure for rate cuts
shared_foundation.summary: All framings accept that 30-year mortgage rates exceeded 7%, that this is mechanically linked to 10-year Treasury yields and Fed policy, that pandemic-era sub-3% rates were historically anomalous, and that housing inventory has tightened. They diverge sharply on causation (Fed vs. geopolitics vs. supply), on whether this is crisis or normalization, and on which policy lever (monetary, fiscal, zoning, supply) should be the focus.

framings.name: Generational Affordability Crisis
framings.question: Who is being locked out of homeownership, and how deep is the harm to their financial futures?
framings.key_claim: 7% mortgage rates, compounded by record home prices, have made homeownership structurally unattainable for millennials and first-time buyers in a way that will define generational wealth inequality.
framings.description: This framing centers the human cost on younger and lower-income would-be buyers, arguing that the rate milestone is not merely a market fluctuation but a structural barrier that widens the wealth gap between existing homeowners and renters.
framings.emphasizes: Monthly payment shock, generational wealth gap, first-time buyer exclusion, the compounding effect of high prices AND high rates simultaneously
framings.downplays: Macroeconomic rationale for rate hikes, historical context showing rates were higher in the 1980s–90s, the role of supply constraints vs. rate levels
sample_headlines: Mortgage rates at 7% a 'tragedy' for homebuyers
Mortgage rates top 7% as housing affordability crisis deepens

carriers.name: Redfin CEO Glenn Kelman / Yahoo Finance
carriers.excerpt: 'It's a tragedy… We pulled the ladder up just as millennials were coming of home-buying age'
carriers.role_evidence: Kelman coined the 'tragedy' framing and the generational ladder metaphor, widely picked up by financial media

carriers.name: Benzinga
carriers.excerpt: The U.S. housing market is grappling with its worst affordability crisis in nearly 40 years.
carriers.role_evidence: Early financial-media amplifier framing 7% rates as a 40-year affordability nadir

carriers.name: CBS News
carriers.excerpt: Higher borrowing costs and elevated residential real estate prices have made home buying unaffordable for a larger swath of buyers
carriers.role_evidence: Broadcast network coverage drove mass-audience adoption of the affordability-crisis frame

carriers.name: WFLX / Gray DC
carriers.excerpt: First-time buyers face rising costs as economy weighs on voters ahead of November elections
carriers.role_evidence: Local TV syndication of Gray DC report spread the generational-affordability frame to regional audiences nationwide

carriers.name: Fortune
carriers.excerpt: Rates approaching 7% could push more people to delay buying a house in an already squeezed market.
carriers.role_evidence: High-traffic business outlet amplifying the buyer-exclusion narrative ahead of the 7% crossing

framings.name: War-Driven Inflation Accountability
framings.question: Did the Trump administration's decision to go to war with Iran directly cause mortgage rates to spike, and who bears political responsibility?
framings.key_claim: The U.S. war with Iran drove up oil prices and inflation expectations, which pushed bond yields and mortgage rates above 7%, making the White House—not the Fed—the proximate cause.
framings.description: This framing draws a direct causal line from the February 2026 Iran conflict to rising energy prices, inflation, bond-market anxiety, and ultimately the 7% mortgage rate, assigning political blame to the Trump administration's foreign policy decision.
framings.emphasizes: The timing correlation between the Iran war start and rate climb, dollar-cost calculations for typical buyers, Trump's 2024 campaign promises on housing costs
framings.downplays: Pre-existing inflationary pressures, the Fed's independent role, structural housing supply deficits
sample_headlines: Mortgage Rates Climb Back Above 7% Due To Trump's Inflation
Trump's War in Iran Is Increasing Mortgage Rates
NEW: Mortgage Rates Hit Nine-Month High, as Trump's Trade War and War With Iran Make Homeownership a Pipe Dream

carriers.name: Center for American Progress
carriers.excerpt: The Trump administration's reckless war of choice in Iran is spreading death and destruction, and American consumers are also seeing rising prices
carriers.role_evidence: CAP published the first detailed dollar-cost analysis linking the Iran war to mortgage rate increases, establishing the causal narrative

carriers.name: Democratic National Committee
carriers.excerpt: Donald Trump's reckless trade war and war with Iran have sent prices through the roof, worsening the housing crisis
carriers.role_evidence: The DNC formally adopted this framing in official party communications, institutionalizing it as a campaign message

carriers.name: Capitol Dispatch (Substack)
carriers.excerpt: Mortgage rates rose back above 7% for the first time since early 2025, up from under 6% before the Iran war began
carriers.role_evidence: Independent newsletter amplifying the Iran-war-to-mortgage-rate causal chain with specific before/after rate comparisons

carriers.name: NPR
carriers.excerpt: Rates have climbed more than a full percentage point since the U.S. war against Iran started.
carriers.role_evidence: NPR's headline explicitly linked the rate milestone to the Iran war start, reaching a large public-radio audience

carriers.name: AOL Finance / MaddowBlog
carriers.excerpt: Mortgage rates reach 7%, despite Trump's misguided 2024 campaign promises
carriers.role_evidence: Explicitly tied the rate milestone to broken campaign promises, amplifying the political-accountability angle

framings.name: Fed Policy & Bond Market Mechanics
framings.question: What macroeconomic and monetary-policy forces actually drive mortgage rates, and is the Fed's tightening cycle working as intended?
framings.key_claim: Mortgage rates above 7% are the direct result of the Fed's inflation-fighting rate hikes and surging 10-year Treasury yields, which are functioning as designed even if painful for housing.
framings.description: This framing treats the 7% rate as a predictable, technically explicable outcome of monetary policy transmission through bond markets, emphasizing the Fed's mandate and the mechanics of how Treasury yields flow into mortgage pricing.
framings.emphasizes: 10-year Treasury yield as the proximate driver, Fed's inflation mandate, MBS spread dynamics, the distinction between the federal funds rate and mortgage rates
framings.downplays: Political culpability, human cost to individual buyers, structural supply-side factors
sample_headlines: Mortgage rates break past 7% as bond yields surge, deepening U.S. housing gridlock
Mortgage rates stay near 7% with Fed, Treasury moves in focus
What Determines the Rate on a 30-Year Mortgage?

carriers.name: Fannie Mae Research
carriers.excerpt: The Federal Reserve's balance sheet actions are the main factor driving the difference in the secondary spread.
carriers.role_evidence: Fannie Mae's institutional research established the authoritative technical explanation of what drives mortgage rates beyond the Fed funds rate

carriers.name: Dallas Fed / Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
carriers.excerpt: The Treasury maturity that most closely resembles the duration characteristics of a mortgage is seven to 10 years
carriers.role_evidence: Federal Reserve regional bank publishing technical analysis of mortgage rate drivers, lending institutional credibility to the bond-market mechanics frame

carriers.name: NPR / Scott Horsley
carriers.excerpt: Mortgages are typically pegged to the rate on 10-year government bonds, and that 10-year Treasury yield has jumped sharply
carriers.role_evidence: NPR's explainer-style coverage foregrounded bond-market mechanics over political blame, reaching a broad public audience

carriers.name: HousingWire
carriers.excerpt: Analysts tie mortgage rates near 7% to Fed inflation concerns and Treasury buyback plans
carriers.role_evidence: Industry trade publication consistently framing rate moves through monetary-policy and bond-market lens for professional housing audience

carriers.name: Axios
carriers.excerpt: The flip side of more rapid U.S. growth is higher long-term interest rates, with homebuyers particularly poised to take it on the chin.
carriers.role_evidence: Axios framed the rate rise as a byproduct of strong economic growth and bond-market dynamics, not political failure

carriers.name: Bankrate
carriers.excerpt: As the funds rate grew, so did mortgage rates, with the 30-year rate breaching 8 percent in October 2023.
carriers.role_evidence: Consumer finance outlet providing ongoing technical context on Fed-to-mortgage transmission

framings.name: Housing Supply Structural Failure
framings.question: Would lower mortgage rates even solve the housing crisis, or is chronic underbuilding and zoning dysfunction the root cause?
framings.key_claim: The 7% rate is a symptom, not the disease: decades of restrictive zoning, NIMBYism, and underbuilding have created a structural supply deficit that makes housing unaffordable regardless of interest rates.
framings.description: This framing argues that focusing on mortgage rates misdiagnoses the problem. The real crisis is a multi-million-unit housing shortage caused by land-use regulation, post-2008 construction collapse, and local political resistance to density—issues that rate cuts alone cannot fix.
framings.emphasizes: Inventory deficit, zoning and land-use barriers, NIMBYism, the lock-in effect of existing owners, the need for supply-side reform
framings.downplays: The immediate pain of rate increases, monetary policy choices, political blame
sample_headlines: Don't let this housing crisis go to waste
Addressing the Housing Affordability Crisis Requires Increasing Housing Supply
Why America's housing crisis has hit a new inflection point

carriers.name: Axios / Neil Irwin
carriers.excerpt: The only solution is more supply, but it won't be forthcoming as long as homebuilders are skittish about rates and affordability.
carriers.role_evidence: Axios framed the 7%+ rate environment as exposing a pre-existing supply failure, not creating a new one

carriers.name: CBRE Investment Management
carriers.excerpt: A complicated web of local, state and federal regulations, particularly around zoning, continue to be the greatest obstacle to increasing supply.
carriers.role_evidence: Institutional real-estate research explicitly named regulation—not rates—as the primary obstacle, establishing the supply-structural frame

carriers.name: Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP)
carriers.excerpt: Policymakers should act aggressively to promote supply increases in places that need more homes.
carriers.role_evidence: Left-leaning policy institution formally adopting the supply-first frame, showing its cross-ideological appeal

carriers.name: The Hill (Opinion)
carriers.excerpt: Overly restrictive zoning, cautious lending and anti-development politics created a long freeze in housing production
carriers.role_evidence: Op-ed in high-traffic political outlet amplifying the zoning-reform supply narrative to a broad policy audience

carriers.name: Congressional Research Service
carriers.excerpt: Increasing regulatory costs, restrictive zoning and land use, and changing demographics have contributed to supply issues.
carriers.role_evidence: Nonpartisan congressional research body formally documenting the supply-structural diagnosis, lending bipartisan institutional weight

carriers.name: Freddie Mac / Sam Khater
carriers.excerpt: 'Demand has been impacted by affordability headwinds, but low inventory remains the root cause of stalling home sales'
carriers.role_evidence: Freddie Mac's chief economist explicitly pushed back on rate-centric narratives by naming inventory as the root cause

framings.name: Frozen Market / Lock-In Effect
framings.question: How does the rate environment trap both buyers and sellers, and what does market paralysis mean for the broader economy?
framings.key_claim: 7% rates have created a 'golden handcuff' lock-in effect where existing owners refuse to sell their low-rate mortgages, choking inventory and paradoxically keeping prices high even as demand falls.
framings.description: This framing focuses on the market-mechanics paradox: high rates simultaneously suppress buyer demand and seller supply, creating a frozen, low-transaction market where prices don't fall as expected. It is primarily an economic and real-estate-industry lens.
framings.emphasizes: Rate lock-in among existing homeowners, inventory collapse, transaction volume decline, the self-reinforcing freeze dynamic
framings.downplays: Political causation, generational equity concerns, long-term structural supply issues
sample_headlines: Mortgage rates top 7%, dealing a further blow to the frozen housing market
Mortgage rates break past 7% as bond yields surge, deepening U.S. housing gridlock
America's housing affordability crisis makes a comeback

carriers.name: CNN / Matt Egan
carriers.excerpt: Mortgage rates reached a grim milestone this week, topping 7% for the first time since January 2025 and reaching their highest level during either of Donald Trump's presidential terms.
carriers.role_evidence: CNN's 'frozen housing market' headline framing was widely syndicated and set the dominant media narrative for the week

carriers.name: Axios
carriers.excerpt: Spiking mortgage rates and high home prices — a dreadful combination that brought America's housing market to a standstill
carriers.role_evidence: Axios introduced the 'standstill' / frozen-market framing in early 2024, before it became the dominant media shorthand

carriers.name: Bright MLS / Lisa Sturtevant
carriers.excerpt: 'The 7% threshold is a foreboding psychological barrier' that could create 'a chilling effect on the market'
carriers.role_evidence: Sturtevant's 'psychological barrier' and 'chilling effect' language was quoted across virtually every major outlet, originating the freeze metaphor

carriers.name: Bloomberg
carriers.excerpt: This was supposed to be the year that sidelined US homebuyers got some relief.
carriers.role_evidence: Bloomberg's explainer framed the 7% crossing as a betrayal of market expectations, amplifying the frozen-market narrative to financial audiences

carriers.name: Mortgage Bankers Association / Mike Fratantoni
carriers.excerpt: 'Potential homebuyers are quite sensitive to these rate changes, as affordability is strained with both higher rates and higher home values'
carriers.role_evidence: MBA's trade data on collapsing application volumes provided the empirical backbone for the frozen-market framing

framings.name: Historical Normalization / Rates Are Not Exceptional
framings.question: Are 7% mortgage rates actually historically unusual, or have buyers and media lost perspective after a decade of anomalously cheap money?
framings.key_claim: 7% mortgage rates are close to the long-run historical average and the real anomaly was the sub-3% pandemic era; the current pain reflects a return to normal, not a crisis.
framings.description: This framing contextualizes the 7% rate against the full historical record—where the 50-year average is near 7.7%—arguing that the crisis narrative is partly a product of recency bias after an unprecedented era of near-zero rates.
framings.emphasizes: Long-run historical average rates, the abnormality of 2020–2021 sub-3% rates, the fact that 7% is below the 1980s–90s norm
framings.downplays: The compounding effect of today's much higher home prices, generational wealth effects, the structural supply deficit
sample_headlines: Mortgage Rate History: Chart & Trends Over Time
30-Year Fixed Mortgage Rate Holds Stable at 7% After Fed Hike
'Expect 7% as the new normal'

carriers.name: The Mortgage Reports
carriers.excerpt: Between April 1971 and February 2026, 30-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 7.70%.
carriers.role_evidence: Mortgage industry publication consistently publishing the long-run average data that anchors the normalization argument

carriers.name: Lawrence Yun / National Association of Realtors
carriers.excerpt: 'Expect 7% as the new normal. Job additions will be the one factor that can support homebuying'
carriers.role_evidence: NAR's chief economist publicly normalized 7% rates, lending institutional credibility to the recalibration frame

carriers.name: Norada Real Estate Investments
carriers.excerpt: The 30-year fixed mortgage rate is holding near 7% after the Fed's 25 bp hike, largely because markets had already priced in the move.
carriers.role_evidence: Real-estate investment media framing 7% as a stable, priced-in equilibrium rather than a shock

carriers.name: NAR Principal Economist Nadia Evangelou
carriers.excerpt: 'I don't think 7% will stop the market'
carriers.role_evidence: NAR researcher explicitly pushed back on the crisis framing, arguing 7% is not a market-stopper

carriers.name: CNN / context paragraph
carriers.excerpt: Mortgage rates remain well below the 7.79% peak they hit in 2023, when inflation was running at decades-high levels.
carriers.role_evidence: Even crisis-framed outlets included historical context paragraphs that partially normalized the 7% level

framings.name: Trump vs. Fed Political Conflict
framings.question: Is the White House's pressure on the Federal Reserve to cut rates appropriate, and who is responsible for the political standoff over monetary policy?
framings.key_claim: The 7% mortgage rate has become a proxy battleground between a president demanding rate cuts and an independent Fed resisting political interference, raising questions about central bank independence.
framings.description: This framing treats the rate milestone as a symptom of a constitutional and institutional conflict between the executive branch and the Federal Reserve, with mortgage rates as the visible casualty of that standoff.
framings.emphasizes: Trump's public demands for rate cuts, Fed Chair Warsh's hawkish stance, the tension between political and monetary authority, the independence of the central bank
framings.downplays: The underlying inflation data driving Fed decisions, the structural housing supply problem, the human cost to individual buyers
sample_headlines: Mortgage rates jump after Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks
Benchmark mortgage rate tops 7 percent, highest in 2 years

carriers.name: The Hill
carriers.excerpt: Trump has urged the FOMC to slash interest rates, which indirectly impact mortgage rates.
carriers.role_evidence: The Hill's widely-syndicated report explicitly juxtaposed Trump's rate-cut demands with the Fed's hike, framing the conflict for a political audience

carriers.name: CNN / Matt Egan
carriers.excerpt: Trump placed the blame for the subsequent rise in mortgage rates squarely on the Fed's shoulders.
carriers.role_evidence: CNN foregrounded the Trump-Fed blame dynamic as a key narrative thread in its flagship rate coverage

carriers.name: HousingWire
carriers.excerpt: This week's increases were largely tied to comments made Friday by Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh at the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium.
carriers.role_evidence: Industry trade outlet tracking the Warsh-Trump friction as a market-moving variable for housing professionals

carriers.name: Norada Real Estate / context note
carriers.excerpt: For the political and policy backdrop behind the hike, see the unanimous Fed hike and Trump–Warsh interest-rate friction.
carriers.role_evidence: Real-estate investment media acknowledging the Trump-Warsh political dimension as relevant context for rate forecasting

framings.name: Geopolitical Risk Premium
framings.question: How much of the mortgage rate increase is attributable to war-driven energy inflation and bond-market risk repricing, independent of domestic policy?
framings.key_claim: The Iran conflict injected a geopolitical risk premium into oil markets and inflation expectations that mechanically transmitted into Treasury yields and mortgage rates, a dynamic that transcends any single administration's policy choices.
framings.description: This framing treats the rate rise as primarily a function of global energy markets and investor risk-repricing in response to the Iran war, positioning it as an external shock rather than a domestic policy failure or political choice.
framings.emphasizes: Oil price transmission to inflation, bond-market investor behavior, the 10-year Treasury yield surge, the war as an exogenous shock
framings.downplays: Pre-existing domestic inflation, the administration's decision to initiate the conflict, structural housing supply issues
sample_headlines: Continued Iran conflict raises mortgage rate risk into late 2026
Why US Homebuyers Are Facing 7% Mortgage Rates Again

carriers.name: HousingWire / Logan Mohtashami
carriers.excerpt: A longer Iran conflict could keep energy prices and inflation elevated, pushing the Fed toward a more hawkish stance.
carriers.role_evidence: HousingWire published the first detailed scenario analysis of how Iran war duration would mechanically affect mortgage rate trajectories

carriers.name: Bloomberg
carriers.excerpt: Then, the Iran war and fears about rising inflation came along.
carriers.role_evidence: Bloomberg's explainer framed the Iran war as the key exogenous shock disrupting what was expected to be a year of rate relief

carriers.name: Quartz (qz.com)
carriers.excerpt: The conflict with Iran has also contributed to higher oil prices and renewed inflation concerns, feeding upward pressure on bond yields
carriers.role_evidence: Quartz explicitly traced the geopolitical transmission mechanism from Iran conflict to oil to inflation to bond yields to mortgage rates

carriers.name: Briefs.co
carriers.excerpt: The climb started back in February, when the outbreak of the Iran war lifted energy costs and revived inflation worries.
carriers.role_evidence: Financial news aggregator presenting the geopolitical-shock framing as the primary causal explanation for the rate climb

carriers.name: NPR / Scott Horsley
carriers.excerpt: The rising prices of fuel, groceries - everything else - was reflected in the turbulent government bond market this week.
carriers.role_evidence: NPR's radio report traced the geopolitical-to-bond-market transmission chain for a mass public audience

gap_analysis: Missing: the construction industry's perspective on how higher rates affect builder margins, labor demand, and project viability—distinct from supply-side housing shortage arguments. Missing: international capital flows and foreign investor behavior (who may be pulling out or doubling down on US real estate). Missing: the positive framing that higher rates restore saver incentives and reduce speculative excess. Missing: regional/sectoral variation—how rates differentially impact rural vs. urban markets, commercial vs. residential, or specific metros with different affordability baselines.
